title: Analytical Investigation Of Two-Spin Entanglement Generated By Different Types Of Bosonic Environments
authors: A. R. Kuzmak A. I. Smetana
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28898v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Due to the rapid development of research in the field of quantum physics and quantum information over the past decades, the need to study physical models that can effectively implement quantum computing has increased. An integral part of such models is the environment, which, on the one hand, leads to decoherence in the system, and on the other hand, generates interaction between spins, which in turn allows for the induction of entanglement, which is an integral part of many quantum algorithms. Therefore, it is essential to investigate the impact of the environment on the behavior of quantum systems, enabling the effective implementation of quantum information devices. Here, we consider the time evolution of two spins generated by the interaction through a bosonic environment. The behavior of negativity as a measure of entanglement between spins is studied for different models of environment. As a result, conditions on the parameters of the environment are obtained to achieve the maximum values of entanglement between spins. In this case, environmental models were obtained that minimize the decoherence of the system while maximizing its entanglement. It became possible to derive an effective unitary operator describing the corresponding evolution, since the influence of decoherence was negligibly small.
tldr: This paper analytically studies how two spins become entangled via a common bosonic environment, identifying conditions that maximize entanglement while minimizing decoherence.
motivation: Understanding how environments can generate entanglement is crucial for quantum information processing, as decoherence typically degrades quantum states. The authors aim to find environmental parameters that enhance entanglement rather than destroy it.
method: The authors model two spins interacting through a bosonic bath and use negativity as an entanglement measure. They derive effective unitary evolution for different environmental models (e.g., Ohmic, sub-Ohmic, super-Ohmic) and analyze the time-dependent entanglement.
result: They obtain conditions on the environment parameters (e.g., spectral density exponent, cutoff frequency) that yield maximal entanglement and minimal decoherence. For certain models, the decoherence becomes negligible, allowing an effective unitary description.
conclusion: The work provides a pathway to engineer bosonic environments that generate strong spin-spin entanglement with low decoherence, which could benefit quantum communication and quantum computing implementations.

title: Hardware-Tailored Resource Estimation For Magic-State Distillation On Silicon Spin Qubits
authors: Songqinghao Yang, Christopher K. Long, Rub\'en M. Otxoa, Prakash Murali, Crispin H. W. Barnes, David R. M. Arvidsson-Shukur
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a resource analysis for generating high-fidelity logical magic states on silicon spin-qubit platforms. We consider a range of architectures, including a shuttling-based SpinBus design, a dense nearest-neighbor layout, and a hybrid scheme with shuttling-connected patches. We compare surface, color, and biased error-correcting codes, and analyze the [MATH] and [MATH] magic-state distillation protocols. Our approach combines bottom-up and top-down methodologies. We construct a hardware-level noise model based on a silicon-processor Hamiltonian with realistic parameters and [MATH] non-Markovian noise, enabling estimation of physical resources required to reach target logical error rates. These results are propagated to system-level overheads for applications including spin dynamics, integer factorization, and quantum chemistry. Conversely, we fix target logical fidelities and derive corresponding constraints on hardware performance. Our framework enables systematic evaluation of resource-reduction strategies. We find that optimized control pulses reduce magic-state distillation overhead by 42\% compared to standard gate implementations. In addition, silicon-tailored biased error-correcting codes achieve an approximately threefold reduction in physical footprint relative to the surface code, even without physical-bias-preserving operations.
tldr: This paper provides a hardware-tailored resource estimation for magic-state distillation on silicon spin qubits, comparing codes and protocols to reduce overhead.
motivation: To enable fault-tolerant quantum computing on silicon spin qubits, high-fidelity magic states are needed, but distillation is resource-intensive. This work aims to optimize resource usage by tailoring distillation to specific hardware architectures.
method: The authors combine bottom-up hardware noise modeling (using a silicon-processor Hamiltonian with non-Markovian noise) with top-down system-level overhead analysis. They evaluate surface, color, and biased codes, and two distillation protocols, across shuttling-based, dense nearest-neighbor, and hybrid architectures.
result: Optimized control pulses reduce distillation overhead by 42%, and silicon-tailored biased codes achieve a threefold reduction in physical footprint compared to the surface code, even without physical-bias-preserving operations.
conclusion: The framework enables systematic evaluation of resource-reduction strategies for magic-state distillation on silicon spin qubits, with significant practical improvements demonstrated.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Zero-Error Communication And Storage Under Positional Uncertainty
authors: Arnau Diebra, David Gonz\'alez-Lociga, Mark Hillery, John Calsamiglia, Emili Bagan
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28945v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Permutation channels model communication and storage scenarios in which the positional identity of the physical carriers is partially or completely lost, so that the transmitted information is only accessible up to an unknown reordering. Here we show that quantum mechanics can dramatically enhance zero-error communication through such channels. For cyclic reorderings of [MATH] [MATH]-level systems, and in the absence of positional metadata, the number of classical zero-error messages scales asymptotically as [MATH], whereas quantum protocols can fully recover the identity-channel value [MATH]. Ancilla-assisted protocols further increase this number to [MATH], enabling dense coding under positional uncertainty. We also analyze dihedral permutation channels and derive general P\'olya-like formulas for the number of distinguishable messages in a broad class of permutation groups. Finally, for the symmetric group [MATH], corresponding to complete scrambling of the information carriers, the number of distinguishable messages scales as [MATH] classically, compared with [MATH] for quantum protocols and [MATH] in the ancilla-assisted setting. Our results establish a fundamental quantum advantage for communication and storage under positional uncertainty.
tldr: Quantum protocols achieve exponentially larger zero-error communication capacity than classical ones under positional uncertainty, with ancilla-assisted schemes enabling dense coding.
motivation: Permutation channels model realistic scenarios where the order of information carriers is lost, limiting classical communication. The goal is to explore whether quantum resources can overcome this limitation.
method: The authors analyze permutation channels for cyclic and dihedral groups, deriving asymptotic scaling of distinguishable messages using combinatorial and group-theoretic methods (Pólya-like formulas). They compare classical, quantum, and ancilla-assisted protocols.
result: For cyclic reorderings, classical messages scale as ~2^n, quantum as ~d^n (full identity channel), and ancilla-assisted as ~(d^2)^n. For symmetric group (complete scrambling), classical scales as ~n^d, quantum as ~d^n, ancilla-assisted as ~(d^2)^n.
conclusion: Quantum mechanics provides a dramatic advantage for zero-error communication under positional uncertainty, with implications for quantum storage and communication networks. Future work may extend to other groups and practical implementations.

title: Collective Radiative Enhancement Of Rare-Earth Ions In Lithium Niobate Via Engineered LargeArea Nanohole Arrays
authors: Ali Najjar Amiri, Trevor Kling, David Barton, Mahdi Hosseini
abstract: ArXiv:2605.29015v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional approaches to light-matter interactions rely on engineering photonic density of states. More recently, tailoring the spatial geometry of atoms or emitters themselves has emerged as a powerful and complementary route to control collective radiative properties. Here we experimentally realize a geometry-engineered ensemble of rare-earth ions by fabricating a periodic array of subwavelength gold nanoholes on lithium niobate implanted with thulium ions, forming a semi-two-dimensional array of quantum emitters embedded in a high-index crystalline thin film. The hybrid structure can simultaneously support localized and lattice plasmon resonances from the metallic array and collective atomic resonances from the ion ensemble. Using time-resolved photoluminescence and temperature-dependent measurements, we observe enhanced radiative emission attributed to collective atomic effects mediated by the nanohole lattice, distinct from single-emitter Purcell enhancement. Our results demonstrate a new regime of light-matter interaction opening a pathway toward broadband and scalable, geometry-controlled quantum optical interfaces in solid-state platforms.
tldr: This paper demonstrates collective radiative enhancement of rare-earth ions in lithium niobate using engineered nanohole arrays, realizing a geometry-controlled quantum optical interface.
motivation: To explore geometry-engineered emitter arrays as a complementary approach to photonic density-of-states engineering for controlling collective radiative properties in solid-state platforms.
method: Fabrication of a periodic array of subwavelength gold nanoholes on lithium niobate implanted with thulium ions, forming a semi-2D emitter array. Time-resolved photoluminescence and temperature-dependent measurements were used to characterize the emission.
result: Enhanced radiative emission attributed to collective atomic effects mediated by the nanohole lattice, distinct from single-emitter Purcell enhancement.
conclusion: The results open a pathway toward broadband, scalable, geometry-controlled quantum optical interfaces in solid-state platforms, relevant for quantum communication and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Partial Entropy Production Of Active Particles With Hidden States In Potentials
authors: Gunnar Pruessner Jacob Knight
abstract: ArXiv:2605.29201v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Partially observed stochastic systems can appear (almost) time-reversal symmetric while in fact operating far from equilibrium. The present work extends the perturbative framework introduced in [Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 198302 (2026)] to calculate in a generic confining potential the partial entropy production, which quantifies the time-reversal asymmetry of a generic active particle with hidden self-propulsion. Focusing on the harmonic case, we apply our framework to reproduce an exact result for the partial entropy production rate of an active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle and to derive the partial entropy production rate of a run-and-tumble particle.
tldr: This paper extends a perturbative framework to compute partial entropy production for active particles with hidden states in confining potentials, quantifying time-reversal asymmetry in partially observed nonequilibrium systems.
motivation: To understand how partially observed stochastic systems can appear time-reversal symmetric while operating far from equilibrium, and to quantify the hidden dissipation in active matter.
method: Extends a perturbative framework from [Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 198302 (2026)] to generic confining potentials, then applies it to harmonic potentials to derive exact results for active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck and run-and-tumble particles.
result: Derives the partial entropy production rate for active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particles (reproducing exact result) and for run-and-tumble particles, showing how hidden self-propulsion contributes to apparent time-reversal asymmetry.
conclusion: Provides a systematic method to infer hidden entropy production in active systems, with implications for understanding energy consumption in nonequilibrium processes and possibly for quantum information thermodynamics.

title: Fundamental Limitations On Entanglement Extraction From Purity
authors: Tulja Varun Kondra, Pedro Barrios Hita, Justus Neumann, Hermann Kampermann, Dagmar Bru{\ss}
abstract: ArXiv:2605.29197v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: States of sufficiently low purity are separable and cannot be entangled by unital (purity-non-generating) operations. Since high-purity states are experimentally demanding, it is natural to ask how much purity a state must possess to enable entanglement generation. Absolutely separable states remain separable under all deterministic unital channels, and so cannot deterministically generate entanglement in this setting. We show, however, that some absolutely separable states can generate entanglement via probabilistic protocols that do not produce purity. This motivates the study of states that fail to generate entanglement with any non-zero probability, which we call completely absolutely separable; we give a full characterization of this class. Along the way, we derive a novel sufficient condition for separability that depends only on the largest and smallest eigenvalues, along with the smallest local dimension and is independent of all previously known spectral separability criteria.
tldr: This paper characterizes states that cannot generate entanglement via probabilistic unital operations, introducing 'completely absolutely separable' states and a new spectral separability criterion.
motivation: To understand the minimal purity required for entanglement generation, especially under probabilistic protocols, and to identify states that are fundamentally incapable of producing entanglement.
method: The authors use mathematical analysis of quantum states and unital channels, deriving necessary and sufficient conditions for complete absolute separability, and proving a new spectral separability criterion based on extremal eigenvalues and local dimension.
result: They show that some absolutely separable states can generate entanglement probabilistically, but a subset called completely absolutely separable states cannot generate entanglement with any nonzero probability; they fully characterize this class and derive a novel sufficient condition for separability.
conclusion: The findings deepen the understanding of the interplay between purity and entanglement, with implications for quantum information processing under realistic noisy conditions, and suggest new directions for exploring operational limitations in entanglement generation.

title: Quantum And Thermal Properties Of The Klein-Gordon Inverted Harmonic Oscillator With Physical Applications
authors: Kevin Hern\'andez
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28875v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a systematic framework for the quantum and thermal properties of a Klein-Gordon scalar field subject to an inverted harmonic potential [MATH]. Starting from a non-Hermitian momentum substitution [MATH], we employ a symplectic phase-space rotation [MATH] to map the system onto an analytically tractable effective harmonic oscillator evaluated at [MATH]. This allows us to define a well-regulated partition function [MATH] and derive closed-form expressions for the free energy, entropy, and thermal correlation functions. We then apply this framework to three physical settings: (i) scalar field fluctuations during cosmological inflation, (ii) quantum fields near black-hole horizons, and (iii) order-parameter dynamics near second-order phase transitions in condensed matter. Our results unify previously scattered results in the literature and provide new predictions for the finite-temperature spectral density and entanglement entropy of unstable quantum systems.
tldr: The paper develops a framework for the Klein-Gordon inverted harmonic oscillator and applies it to cosmology, black holes, and phase transitions, with implications for finite-temperature spectral density and entanglement entropy.
motivation: To unify scattered results on unstable quantum systems and provide new predictions for finite-temperature properties and entanglement entropy.
method: Uses a non-Hermitian momentum substitution and symplectic phase-space rotation to map the inverted harmonic oscillator to an effective harmonic oscillator, enabling closed-form expressions for thermodynamic quantities.
result: Derives well-regulated partition function, free energy, entropy, and thermal correlation functions; applies to scalar field fluctuations during inflation, near black-hole horizons, and near second-order phase transitions.
conclusion: Provides a unified framework for unstable quantum systems with applications to cosmology, black holes, and condensed matter, and offers new predictions for finite-temperature spectral density and entanglement entropy.

title: Atom--photon Entanglement With A Single Trapped Cesium Atom
authors: H. Hwang, J. Moon, F. Herzallah, E. Oh, A. Safari, M. Saffman
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28968v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate atom--photon entanglement using a single cesium atom trapped in an optical tweezer. Entanglement is generated by resonant excitation and subsequent spontaneous decay, which entangles the atomic Zeeman state with photon polarization. The photon is collected with a high numerical aperture objective (NA = 0.55) and coupled into a single-mode fiber, enabling atom photon measurements and measurement of the Bell-state fidelity. We obtain raw entanglement fidelity of [MATH] and inferred fidelity of [MATH] after correcting independently characterized atom measurement errors. Compared with related free-space experiments using [MATH]Rb, the multilevel structure of the relevant excited state in [MATH]Cs requires the use of a single short excitation pulse in each entanglement attempt in order to suppress unwanted re-excitation. These results establish a free-space Cs atom--photon interface and provide a step toward dual-species Rb--Cs quantum networking.
tldr: Demonstrates atom-photon entanglement using a single cesium atom in an optical tweezer, achieving high fidelity and establishing a free-space Cs atom-photon interface for quantum networking.
motivation: To create a reliable atom-photon entanglement source for quantum networks, particularly for dual-species Rb-Cs networking, and to address challenges with multilevel structure in Cs.
method: A single Cs atom is trapped in an optical tweezer, excited by a resonant pulse, and the spontaneous decay entangles the atomic Zeeman state with photon polarization. Photons are collected via a high NA objective and coupled into a single-mode fiber for Bell-state measurements.
result: Raw entanglement fidelity of [MATH] and inferred fidelity of [MATH] after correcting atom measurement errors. A single short excitation pulse is used to suppress re-excitation in Cs.
conclusion: Establishes a free-space Cs atom-photon interface, enabling steps toward dual-species Rb-Cs quantum networking and potentially improving quantum repeater architectures.

title: Contrast Enhanced Imaging Through Weakly Scattering Media With Spatially Entangled Photons
authors: James Hubble, Rojan Abolhassani, Alessio D'errico, Nazanin Dehghan, Yishai Klein, Yingwen Zhang, Ebrahim Karimi
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28998v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Improving the image contrast of objects immersed in weakly scattering media can be achieved using various strategies. One common approach is to reject events associated with scattered photons in favor of the detection of ballistic photons. While this is traditionally done via time gating or spatial filtering, we propose a different approach based on probing the object with spatio-temporally entangled photon pairs. We show that coincidence detection, followed by post-selection on spatially correlated events, allows us to isolate ballistic from scattered bi-photons, thereby enhancing image contrast relative to a single-photon detection strategy, and simultaneously removes events due to background light. Our predictions are obtained via numerical simulations and confirmed by experiments conducted in two configurations where either both photons or only one illuminates the scene. In both scenarios, correlation post-selection shows an improvement in image contrast at the expense of higher shot noise due to the lower number of events. The latter can be partially compensated for by appropriately combining events from several post-selection windows. Our findings will enable extending imaging through scattering media into the quantum imaging framework in settings where adaptive optics, time gating, and spatial filtering are impractical.
tldr: Using spatially entangled photon pairs and coincidence detection to enhance image contrast in weakly scattering media by rejecting scattered photons.
motivation: To improve imaging through scattering media where traditional methods like time gating or spatial filtering are impractical, by leveraging quantum correlations.
method: Probe object with spatio-temporally entangled photon pairs; perform coincidence detection and post-select on spatially correlated events to isolate ballistic bi-photons.
result: Correlation post-selection improves image contrast compared to single-photon detection, at the cost of higher shot noise, which can be mitigated by combining multiple post-selection windows.
conclusion: Extends quantum imaging to scattering media scenarios where classical techniques fail, with potential for practical quantum-enhanced imaging systems.

title: A Hidden Bottleneck In Classical And Quantum Linear Reservoir Computing
authors: Johannes Nokkala, Federico Centrone, Francesco Arzani
abstract: ArXiv:2605.29071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We identify a hidden bottleneck in the information processing capacity of linear reservoir computers. When the measured features evolve linearly in the reservoir and the output is formed by linear readout with bias, we show that the capacity available at any fixed delay is limited by what is already present in the preprocessed input. Linear reservoir dynamics can therefore redistribute features, but cannot create new fixed-delay expressive power on their own. This limitation is hidden by global capacity measures, since contributions from different delays can accumulate even when each individual delay is strongly constrained. As an experimentally important realization of this general result, we derive the corresponding Gaussian limit for covariance-based continuous-variable quantum reservoirs. Numerical experiments show that experimentally accessible single-photon operations surpass this limit, establishing them as a genuine resource for quantum reservoir computing. The resulting excess capacity also provides an operational witness of non-Gaussian processing in black-box continuous-variable systems under minimal assumptions.
tldr: Linear reservoir computers have a hidden bottleneck: fixed-delay capacity is limited to preprocessed input, but non-Gaussian quantum operations can surpass this limit.
motivation: To uncover fundamental limitations of linear reservoir computing and identify genuine quantum resources for quantum reservoir computing.
method: Theoretical analysis of information capacity in linear reservoirs, derivation of Gaussian limit for covariance-based continuous-variable quantum reservoirs, and numerical experiments with single-photon operations.
result: Linear reservoir dynamics cannot create new fixed-delay expressive power beyond preprocessed input; single-photon operations exceed the Gaussian limit, providing an operational witness of non-Gaussian processing.
conclusion: Non-Gaussian operations are a genuine resource for quantum reservoir computing, and the excess capacity can serve as a witness of non-Gaussianity in black-box continuous-variable systems.

title: Quantum And Classical Noise Characteristics Of Parametrically Driven Cavity Solitons In Dispersive Kerr Resonators
authors: Miro Erkintalo Sophie S. Shamailov
abstract: ArXiv:2605.29321v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temporal cavity solitons generated in monochromatically driven dispersive Kerr resonators offer an attractive avenue for on-chip optical frequency comb generation. Key to many of their applications is to understand how noise -- both technical and quantum -- affects the soliton states, which has accordingly been extensively investigated. Here, we report on a comprehensive theoretical study that elucidates how technical and quantum fluctuations impact a new type of soliton structure that has very recently been predicted and observed in dispersive Kerr resonators under conditions of bichromatic driving: the pure-Kerr parametrically driven cavity soliton (PDCS). We examine how classical laser phase noise transfers from the two pump fields onto the soliton frequency comb, and we calculate the solitons' fundamental quantum-limited timing jitter and two-mode squeezing spectra. In each case, we find that PDCSs can out-perform conventional cavity solitons with comparable characteristics, even when driven by two uncorrelated lasers. Our results demonstrate that pure-Kerr PDCSs can offer unprecedented performance in noise-sensitive photonic applications and as a quantum resource.
tldr: This paper studies noise characteristics of parametrically driven cavity solitons in Kerr resonators, showing they outperform conventional solitons in noise-sensitive applications.
motivation: To understand how technical and quantum noise affect a new type of soliton (PDCS) in bichromatically driven Kerr resonators, which is important for applications like optical frequency combs.
method: Theoretical analysis of classical laser phase noise transfer and calculation of quantum-limited timing jitter and two-mode squeezing spectra for PDCSs.
result: PDCSs exhibit superior noise performance compared to conventional cavity solitons, even when driven by two uncorrelated lasers.
conclusion: PDCSs offer unprecedented performance in noise-sensitive photonic applications and as a quantum resource, with implications for quantum optics and hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Local Description Of Strong Symmetries And Strong-to-weak Symmetry Breaking In Quantum Many-body Systems
authors: Ruizhi Liu, Jinmin Yi, Dominic V. Else
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In mixed states of quantum systems, symmetries come in two types: strong and weak. Furthermore, it has been argued that in quantum many-body systems, strong symmetries can be "spontaneously broken" down to weak symmetries. An issue is that as previously formulated, such "strong-to-weak symmetry breaking" appears to be a fairly non-local effect. In this paper, we show how to understand and diagnose strong symmetries and strong-to-weak symmetry breaking in an explicitly local way. Our main technical tool is a rigorous definition of strong symmetry in the limit of infinite volume, which generalizes the conventional finite-volume definitions, and for which we give several equivalent formulations, including one involving the concept of "local charge coherence". Finally, we introduce von Neumann systems, which in infinite-volume symmetries are intermediate between strong and weak symmetries. We derive a Lieb-Schultz-Mattis type anomaly constraint for von Neumann symmetries (and therefore, in particular, strong symmetries) in quantum spin chains.
tldr: This paper provides a local description of strong symmetries and strong-to-weak symmetry breaking in quantum many-body systems, introducing rigorous infinite-volume definitions and a new intermediate symmetry class.
motivation: Previous formulations of strong-to-weak symmetry breaking appeared non-local; the authors aim to understand and diagnose these phenomena in an explicitly local way.
method: The authors develop a rigorous definition of strong symmetry in the infinite-volume limit, generalizing finite-volume definitions, and introduce the concept of 'local charge coherence'. They also define von Neumann symmetries as an intermediate class and derive a Lieb-Schultz-Mattis type anomaly constraint.
result: They provide several equivalent formulations of strong symmetry, including one based on local charge coherence, and show that von Neumann symmetries are intermediate between strong and weak. An LSM anomaly constraint is derived for von Neumann symmetries in quantum spin chains.
conclusion: The work clarifies the local nature of strong symmetries and symmetry breaking, with implications for understanding mixed-state phases and anomalies in many-body systems.

title: Quantum Crossovers Revealed By Local Measurements
authors: A. C. S. Costa, E. C. Diniz, O. P. de Sa Neto
abstract: ArXiv:2605.29019v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum crossover phenomena play a central role in few-body open quantum systems, yet their identification often relies on global or model-dependent indicators. In this work, we demonstrate that crossovers can be robustly characterized through purely local measurements, establishing a direct connection between local quantum Fisher information and the onset of crossover behavior. We further demonstrate that quantum obesity does not, in general, generalize the quantum steering ellipsoid volume as a universal indicator of crossover. Instead, we identify regimes in which the ellipsoid volume remains insensitive to the transition, while the relevant signatures are encoded in the behavior of the local Bloch vector. These results reveal a geometric distinction between local and global indicators of crossovers.
tldr: Local measurements, specifically local quantum Fisher information, can robustly characterize quantum crossovers in few-body open quantum systems, revealing a geometric distinction between local and global indicators.
motivation: Quantum crossovers are important in few-body open quantum systems but are typically identified using global or model-dependent indicators. This work aims to establish a direct connection between local measurements and crossover behavior.
method: The authors analyze local quantum Fisher information and the quantum steering ellipsoid volume as indicators of crossover behavior in few-body open quantum systems, comparing their sensitivity to transitions.
result: Local quantum Fisher information robustly signals crossovers, while the quantum steering ellipsoid volume is not a universal indicator; in some regimes, the ellipsoid volume remains insensitive, and the crossover is encoded in the local Bloch vector.
conclusion: The results reveal a geometric distinction between local and global indicators, suggesting that local measurements can serve as reliable probes of quantum crossovers, with implications for experimental detection and understanding of quantum phase transitions.

title: A Quantum Algorithm For Simulating Nonunitary Dynamics Governed By Nonautonomous Linear Ordinary Differential Equations
authors: Eitan Geva Pouya Khazaei
abstract: ArXiv:2605.29052v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonautonomous linear ordinary differential equations of the form [MATH], where [MATH] is non-skew-symmetric, are often used to describe nonunitary dynamics in a variety of fields that range from open quantum system dynamics to economic modeling. Because quantum computing hardware is designed to natively implement unitary transformations, existing algorithms for solving such equations on quantum hardware are based on the assumption that the nonunitary propagator is known, and use dilation techniques to embed the nonunitary dynamics within the unitary dynamics of a larger system. However, with the exception of cases where the nonunitary propagator is known in closed form, it needs to be calculated and manipulated on a classical computer at each time step. In this paper, we propose a quantum algorithm that does not require a priori knowledge of the explicit nonunitary propagator and effectively performs the dilation on the quantum hardware. Our algorithm combines a dilation scheme that uses singular value decomposition (SVD) to write the nonunitary propagator as a sum of unitaries with simulating the dynamics of the SVD factors on the quantum hardware. The population-only time-convolutionless quantum master equation describing photoinduced charge transfer in a solvated molecular triad is used as a demonstrative example of the applicability of the algorithm and its sensitivity to noise.
tldr: Proposes a quantum algorithm for simulating nonunitary dynamics governed by nonautonomous linear ODEs without requiring explicit knowledge of the nonunitary propagator, using SVD dilation on quantum hardware.
motivation: Existing quantum algorithms for nonunitary dynamics require prior knowledge of the propagator, which often must be computed classically, limiting efficiency. This work aims to eliminate that bottleneck.
method: Combines a dilation scheme based on singular value decomposition (SVD) to express the nonunitary propagator as a sum of unitaries, then simulates the dynamics of the SVD factors directly on quantum hardware.
result: Demonstrates the algorithm on a population-only time-convolutionless quantum master equation for photoinduced charge transfer in a solvated molecular triad, showing applicability and sensitivity to noise.
conclusion: The algorithm offers a new approach to simulating nonunitary dynamics on quantum computers, with potential applications in open quantum systems and other fields, though noise sensitivity requires further study.

title: Prime Number Identification Demonstrated With Quantum Processors Using A New Rescaling-Based Noise Mitigation Technique
authors: Victor F. Dos Santos, Victor P. Brasil, Pedro A. S. Contri, Jonas Maziero
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28964v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We implement a quantum protocol for prime number identification based on entanglement dynamics, using IBM quantum processors. The method links the primality of an integer to specific Fourier components extracted from the time evolution of entanglement in a bipartite quantum system. To mitigate experimental noise, we introduce a noise-mitigation method based on a global rescaling factor, which is calibrated on a subset of circuits and extrapolated across different configurations. Theoretical support is provided by a new analytical bound for the Fourier modes derived assuming an initial uniform superposition state. This new bound enhances the separation between prime and composite numbers under moderate experimental deviations. These results represent a step toward practical number-theoretic applications on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices.
tldr: This paper uses entanglement dynamics on IBM quantum processors to identify prime numbers, introducing a rescaling-based noise mitigation technique.
motivation: To demonstrate a quantum protocol for prime number identification using entanglement, and to mitigate noise in NISQ devices.
method: The protocol links primality to Fourier components from entanglement evolution; a global rescaling factor is calibrated on a subset of circuits and extrapolated to mitigate noise.
result: A new analytical bound for Fourier modes improves separation between prime and composite numbers; experimental implementation on IBM processors shows feasibility.
conclusion: The work advances number-theoretic applications on NISQ devices, but the noise mitigation technique is specific and may not generalize.

title: Uncertainty Relations In Classical And Quantum Theories Of Electromagnetism
authors: Zofia Bialynicka-Birula Iwo Bialynicki-Birula
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28906v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sharp uncertainty relations restricting the values of variances in the position space and in the momentum (wavevector) space are derived. They have the same form [MATH] in the classical theory of light beams, in the quantum theory of coherent light beams, and in the quantum theory of individual photons.
tldr: Derives sharp uncertainty relations for variances in position and momentum spaces that hold across classical light beams, coherent quantum light, and individual photons.
motivation: To establish rigorous uncertainty relations that apply uniformly to both classical and quantum electromagnetic theories, bridging a gap in the literature.
method: Analytical derivation using the mathematical structure of electromagnetic fields in position and wavevector spaces.
result: Uncertainty relations of the same form are obtained for classical light beams, quantum coherent light, and individual photons.
conclusion: The results unify uncertainty principles across classical and quantum electromagnetism, but do not directly address the user's specific interests in information thermodynamics, quantum communication, or hybrid systems.

title: Learning Quantum Ground States In The Space Of Measurement Outcomes
authors: Kartiek Agarwal
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28931v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate variational learning of quantum many-body ground states directly in measurement space using autoregressive neural networks. In particular, we represent quantum states via probability distributions of outcomes over a symmetric informationally complete positive operator-valued measure (SIC-POVM). The probability distribution is encoded in the parameters of an autoregressive neural-network-based on gated recurrent units (GRUs). Ground states are obtained by gradient descent that updates the probability distribution to minimize the energy with respect to a given Hamiltonian, while enforcing positivity constraints that ensure that the distribution of measurement outcomes correspond to a physical quantum state. We analyze the role of constraint enforcement (hierarchy of positivity conditions), variety of neural network architectures (multiple layers, dilation, and modifications of input data) in determining the success of this approach. We benchmark our approach on one-dimensional transverse-field Ising model and the Heisenberg model, along with gapping fields, for system sizes up to L=128, illustrating its efficacy across a wide variety of models.
tldr: This paper uses autoregressive neural networks to learn quantum ground states from SIC-POVM measurement outcomes, benchmarking on 1D spin models.
motivation: To develop a variational method for learning quantum many-body ground states directly in measurement space, avoiding the need for explicit state representations.
method: Represent quantum states as probability distributions over SIC-POVM outcomes, encoded by a GRU-based autoregressive neural network. Minimize energy via gradient descent while enforcing positivity constraints.
result: The method successfully learns ground states for 1D transverse-field Ising and Heisenberg models up to L=128, with performance depending on constraint enforcement and network architecture.
conclusion: The approach offers a scalable way to represent quantum states in measurement space, but its applicability to higher dimensions and more complex systems remains to be seen.

title: Comparing Classical Simulation And Sample-Based Learning Of Quantum Systems: Learning The Hardness Of Quantum Systems From Samples
authors: Jo\~ao Pedro Del Rey, Ra\'ul O. Vallejos, Fernando de Melo
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28986v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the relationship between two distinct classical approaches to quantum systems: direct simulation from a classical description and sample-based learning from measurement data. While both tasks ultimately aim to reproduce Born-rule statistics, complexity-theoretic results suggest that simulability and learnability need not coincide in general. Here we study this relationship empirically using a fixed deep energy-based generative model trained on measurement samples from controlled families of quantum states. We independently tune two quantum resources associated with classical simulation cost: entanglement, through the bond dimension of random matrix product states, and non-stabilizerness, through the number of T gates in Clifford-dominated circuits. Learning difficulty is characterized using two probes of neural-network complexity: the largest Hessian eigenvalue at convergence and Random Subspace Optimization. For both quantum resources, increasing simulation hardness systematically correlates with sharper loss landscapes and degraded reconstruction performance under constrained capacity. Our results indicate that, within the regimes studied here, classical learnability tracks known simulation complexity measures, suggesting that neural-network training dynamics can provide an empirical probe of quantum computational hardness.
tldr: This paper empirically studies the relationship between classical simulation cost and sample-based learnability of quantum states using neural networks, finding that harder-to-simulate states are also harder to learn.
motivation: To understand whether classical simulability and learnability from measurement data coincide, given complexity-theoretic results suggesting they may not.
method: Train a deep energy-based generative model on measurement samples from random matrix product states (varying entanglement) and Clifford+T circuits (varying non-stabilizerness), then analyze learning difficulty via Hessian eigenvalues and Random Subspace Optimization.
result: Increasing simulation hardness (higher entanglement or more T gates) correlates with sharper loss landscapes and worse reconstruction performance under constrained capacity.
conclusion: Classical learnability tracks known simulation complexity measures in the studied regimes, suggesting neural-network training dynamics can probe quantum computational hardness.

title: Cavity Optomechanics In An Infinite Cylinder
authors: Samar Deep, Emily Eadie, Pablo Bianucci
abstract: ArXiv:2605.29154v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report the observation of optically-induced mechanical oscillations in flame-produced surface nanoscale axial photonic resonators (SNAPRs). The frequency of the optically-excited mechanical modes in these SNAPRs is not affected by the particulars of the optical axial confinement, and matches with the theoretically predicted frequency for the fundamental breathing mode of an infinite solid cylinder. When the SNAPR fabrication recipe is changed, changing the optical mode spectrum, the behaviour of the observed mechanical modes remains unchanged. This shows a degree of geometrical uncoupling between the optical and mechanical degrees of freedom, which in turn implies the effective radius variation causing axial optical confinement in our SNAPRs is dominated by a refractive index change rather than a physical radius change.
tldr: This paper reports optically-induced mechanical oscillations in flame-produced SNAPRs, showing that the mechanical mode frequency matches that of an infinite solid cylinder and is uncoupled from optical confinement, implying the optical confinement is due to refractive index change rather than physical radius variation.
motivation: To understand the coupling between optical and mechanical degrees of freedom in cavity optomechanical systems, specifically in SNAPRs, and to determine the origin of axial optical confinement.
method: Experimental observation of optically-induced mechanical oscillations in SNAPRs; comparison of measured mechanical mode frequencies with theoretical predictions for an infinite solid cylinder; variation of fabrication recipe to change optical mode spectrum while monitoring mechanical modes.
result: The mechanical mode frequency is unaffected by optical axial confinement and matches the fundamental breathing mode of an infinite solid cylinder; changing the optical mode spectrum does not alter mechanical mode behavior, indicating geometrical uncoupling between optical and mechanical degrees of freedom.
conclusion: The effective radius variation causing axial optical confinement in SNAPRs is dominated by a refractive index change rather than a physical radius change, which has implications for designing optomechanical systems with tailored optical and mechanical properties.

title: Polar Fidelities, Holevo Bases, And Unitary Factors Of Generalized Fidelity
authors: Trung Dung Vuong
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28885v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivated by several open problems in the Afham-Ferrie theory of generalized fidelity, we study polar fidelities, Holevo bases, and unitary factors on \(\Pd\), the cone of \(d\times d\) complex positive definite matrices. We prove that, for every fixed pair \(P,Q\in\Pd\), the one-sided polar fidelities \(x\mapsto F_{P^x}(P,Q)\) and \(x\mapsto F_{Q^x}(P,Q)\), as well as their symmetrization, are nondecreasing on \((-\infty,1]\) and nonincreasing on \([1,\infty)\). Hence the polar paths realize exactly the interval \([\FM(P,Q),\FU(P,Q)]\) on \([-1,1]\), yielding pointwise, generally pair-dependent realizations of all \(z\)-fidelity values with \(z\ge1/2\) and of the Log-Euclidean fidelity as generalized fidelities. We also show that for \(d\ge2\) and \(0<1/2\), such realization fails in general, even for interior fidelities. We further solve the fixed-pair Holevo-base equation \(F_R(P,Q)=\FH(P,Q)\), classify all Holevo bases, and classify exactly which unitary factors of generalized fidelity can arise from a base \(R\). These are precisely the unitaries \(W\) for which \(P^{-1/2}Q^{1/2}W\) is similar to a positive definite matrix. This recovers the special-unitary constraint and disproves the global reverse inclusion \(SU(d)\) for \(d\ge2\).
tldr: This paper studies mathematical properties of generalized fidelity, polar fidelities, and Holevo bases on positive definite matrices, with no direct connection to quantum information thermodynamics, foundations, communication, or hybrid systems.
motivation: The research is motivated by open problems in the Afham-Ferrie theory of generalized fidelity, aiming to understand the structure of polar fidelities and unitary factors.
method: The authors use mathematical analysis on the cone of positive definite matrices, proving monotonicity properties of polar fidelities and solving the fixed-pair Holevo-base equation.
result: Key findings include monotonicity of polar fidelities on intervals, realization of z-fidelity values for z≥1/2, classification of Holevo bases, and characterization of unitary factors that can arise from a base.
conclusion: The results provide deeper insight into generalized fidelity but are primarily of mathematical interest, with limited immediate application to the user's research areas.

title: Quantum Encodings That Preserve Persistent Homology
authors: Andrew Vlasic Arthur J. Parzygnat
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28927v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given a data set with a notion of distance, such as a point cloud in Euclidean space, topological data analysis (TDA) uses techniques from algebraic topology and metric geometry to infer the topology of a hypothetical manifold from which the data are sampled. This inference is achieved by calculating topological invariants, some of which are difficult to compute classically. Meanwhile, quantum TDA utilizes quantum processes to extract the invariants used in making such inferences in an attempt to speed up the computations. Because applying transformations to the original classical dataset could alter the associated topological invariants, we investigate which quantum encodings would best preserve the invariants of the original dataset. This line of inquiry is distinct from standard approaches in quantum TDA, whose typical starting point is not from the classical dataset directly, but rather from the associated combinatorial objects, such as simplicial complexes, which typically demand a lot of resources to construct. We take the first step at a more direct approach by focusing on which quantum encodings acting directly on the data are admissible for applying quantum algorithms to extract topological features from classical datasets.
tldr: This paper investigates which quantum encodings of classical data preserve topological invariants for quantum topological data analysis.
motivation: Standard quantum TDA starts from simplicial complexes, which are resource-intensive to construct; the authors aim for a more direct approach by encoding classical data directly into quantum states while preserving persistent homology.
method: The study analyzes different quantum encodings (e.g., amplitude encoding, angle encoding) and evaluates their ability to preserve the persistent homology of the original dataset.
result: The paper identifies which encodings are admissible for preserving topological features, providing a foundation for direct quantum TDA algorithms.
conclusion: This work opens a new direction in quantum TDA by focusing on data encoding, but it is preliminary and does not yet provide practical algorithms or experimental results.

title: Exponentially Fast Solution State Preparation For The Heat Equation And Its Use For Option Pricing
authors: Gumaro Rendon, Stepan Smid, Sarvagya Upadhyay
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28950v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we present the methods necessary to price an important set of derivatives on a quantum device while offering an advantage over existing classical methods. The methods developed here, in conjunction with ~, also provide an exponential advantage in requirement of qubits when pricing some option contracts with path-dependent payoff compared to state-of-the-art quantum Monte Carlo methods.
tldr: This paper presents quantum methods for pricing derivatives with exponential qubit advantage over quantum Monte Carlo, but does not directly address the user's research interests.
motivation: To develop quantum algorithms for option pricing that offer exponential advantage in qubit count for path-dependent options.
method: The authors propose a solution state preparation method for the heat equation, combined with quantum amplitude estimation.
result: Exponential reduction in qubit requirements for pricing certain path-dependent options compared to state-of-the-art quantum Monte Carlo.
conclusion: The methods could enable practical quantum advantage in derivative pricing, but further work is needed for implementation on near-term devices.

title: Local Strong-to-Weak Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking
authors: Francisco Divi, Leonardo A. Lessa, Chong Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28967v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a local notion of strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SW-SSB), through a local one-point fidelity correlator. Compared with the previous definition in terms of a two-point fidelity correlator, our local formulation offers two key advantages: (1) it is easier to detect in large systems: for a system of size [MATH] and with [MATH] amount of resources, one can detect the local fidelity order up to volume scale [MATH]; and (2) the local SW-SSB order remains well defined in the thermodynamic limit, where the density matrix itself is not well defined. We show that key features of SW-SSB, including stability under finite-depth symmetric channels and long-range conditional mutual information, persist within this local framework. Our definition is conceptually analogous to local thermalization, as exemplified by pure states obeying the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH). For critical states, the local one-point fidelity correlator defines an interesting class of defect problems. We demonstrate the applicability of the local formulation through several concrete examples, and derive the universal scaling behavior of the local fidelity correlator in a range of critical systems, including ground states of conformal field theories as well as ballistic and diffusive free-fermion metals.
tldr: The paper introduces a local definition of strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking using a one-point fidelity correlator, improving detectability and thermodynamic limit behavior.
motivation: Previous definitions of SW-SSB relied on two-point fidelity correlators, which are harder to detect in large systems and become ill-defined in the thermodynamic limit. The authors aim to provide a more practical and well-defined local order parameter.
method: The authors propose a local one-point fidelity correlator as an order parameter for SW-SSB, analyze its properties under finite-depth symmetric channels, and derive universal scaling in critical systems using conformal field theory and free-fermion models.
result: The local fidelity correlator is easier to detect (requires O(1) resources for volume-scale detection), remains well-defined in the thermodynamic limit, and captures key features of SW-SSB such as stability under symmetric channels and long-range conditional mutual information. Universal scaling behavior is derived for critical systems.
conclusion: The local formulation provides a robust framework for studying SW-SSB in large and critical systems, with potential applications to quantum error correction and many-body physics.

title: Universal Response Of Rydberg Manifolds To Standing Light Waves From The Microwave To The X-ray Regime
authors: Homar Rivera-Rodr\'iguez, Matthew T. Eiles, Jan M. Rost
abstract: ArXiv:2605.29024v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standing light waves structure the electronic density of a Rydberg atom in a rich but surprisingly systematic fashion. We uncover these systematics, which are nearly universal across a large range of principal quantum numbers n, by varying the wavelength of the standing light over several orders of magnitude. Thereby, we identify five qualitatively different regimes and give their transition criteria in terms of specific critical wavelengths. The bandwidth of the lattice spectrum, manifested in the difference of energies between the states on the edges of the degeneracy-lifted n-manifolds, as well as the organization of the electron density in coordinate and momentum space are used to rationalize the systematics. A experimental setup is proposed to measure the features in the different regimes.
tldr: This paper studies the universal response of Rydberg atoms to standing light waves across a wide range of wavelengths, identifying five regimes based on critical wavelengths.
motivation: To understand how standing light waves structure the electronic density of Rydberg atoms and to uncover systematic, nearly universal behavior across different principal quantum numbers.
method: The authors vary the wavelength of the standing light over several orders of magnitude and analyze the bandwidth of the lattice spectrum and electron density in coordinate and momentum space.
result: Five qualitatively different regimes are identified with transition criteria given by specific critical wavelengths; the energy differences and electron density organization rationalize the systematics.
conclusion: The findings provide a universal framework for Rydberg atoms in standing waves, with an experimental setup proposed to measure features in the different regimes.

title: Local Diagnostics For Strong-to-weak Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking And Non-equilibrium Phase Transitions
authors: Carolyn Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.29113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct strongly [MATH]-symmetric local Markov/Lindblad dynamics exhibiting transitions between strong-paramagnetic behavior and strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking. In 1+1d, an absorbing-state construction gives a transition with scaling consistent with the parity-conserving branching-annihilating random-walk universality class. In 2+1d, a pair-flip variant of Toom's rule provides evidence for a stable strong-paramagnetic/weakly symmetry-broken regime and a transition into an active SWSSB regime. We also introduce a marginal fidelity correlator of radius [MATH], a local proxy for the usual SWSSB fidelity order parameter requiring tomography only on [MATH]-size regions. For broad classes of states, including symmetry-projected Gibbs-like states satisfying suitable local indistinguishability assumptions, we bound the error between the marginal and global fidelity correlators by terms decaying exponentially in [MATH]. These marginal fidelities provide a model-independent diagnostic of SWSSB in absorbing-state transitions, where microscopic notions of defects or activity are not universal.
tldr: This paper studies strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SWSSB) in open quantum systems using local Markov/Lindblad dynamics, introducing a marginal fidelity correlator as a diagnostic.
motivation: To understand non-equilibrium phase transitions and symmetry breaking in open quantum systems, particularly the transition from strong to weak symmetry breaking, and to develop local diagnostics that do not require global tomography.
method: Constructs strongly symmetric local Markov/Lindblad dynamics in 1+1d and 2+1d, using an absorbing-state construction and a pair-flip variant of Toom's rule. Introduces a marginal fidelity correlator and bounds its error relative to the global fidelity order parameter.
result: In 1+1d, the transition scaling matches the parity-conserving branching-annihilating random-walk universality class. In 2+1d, evidence for a stable strong-paramagnetic/weakly symmetry-broken regime and a transition into an active SWSSB regime. The marginal fidelity correlator provides a local diagnostic with exponentially decaying error.
conclusion: The marginal fidelity correlator is a model-independent diagnostic for SWSSB, useful for absorbing-state transitions where microscopic defects are not universal. This work advances the understanding of non-equilibrium phase transitions in open quantum systems.

title: Quantum Error Correction And Fault Tolerance: A Comprehensive Tutorial
authors: Daniel J. Spencer, Shubham P. Jain, Andrew Tanggara, Zeen Sun, Tobias Haug, Derek Khu, Kishor Bharti
abstract: ArXiv:2605.29137v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Noise is one of the central obstacles to building useful quantum computers, and quantum error correction (QEC) provides the framework for protecting quantum information against it. Unlike classical error correction, QEC must preserve fragile quantum states without copying them, measuring them directly, or destroying the information they encode. Driven by rapid progress in both theory and experiment, this challenge has grown into one of the most active areas of quantum information science. This tutorial gives a guided introduction to modern QEC, developing the core concepts of codes, syndromes, stabilizers, decoding, and fault tolerance before connecting them to major code families and current research directions. We cover both established constructions and newer developments, including topological and subsystem codes, bosonic and qudit codes, dynamical codes, and quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes. The emphasis is on building operational understanding: explaining not only what the main objects are, but how they are used in code design, error diagnosis, decoding, and fault-tolerant computation. The tutorial is intended for newcomers seeking a first path through QEC, as well as researchers looking for a coherent reference for the concepts, code families, and tools that arise in current work.
tldr: A comprehensive tutorial on quantum error correction and fault tolerance, covering codes, stabilizers, decoding, and major code families.
motivation: Noise is a central obstacle to building useful quantum computers, and QEC provides the framework to protect quantum information.
method: The tutorial develops core concepts of codes, syndromes, stabilizers, decoding, and fault tolerance, then connects them to major code families and current research directions.
result: Covers both established constructions and newer developments including topological, subsystem, bosonic, qudit, dynamical, and qLDPC codes.
conclusion: Provides an operational understanding for newcomers and a coherent reference for researchers.

title: Modular non-Hermitian Topology And Its Application To Critical Sensing
authors: Saubhik Sarkar, Chiranjib Mukhopadhyay, Abolfazl Bayat
abstract: ArXiv:2605.29173v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-Hermitian topological systems have attracted a lot of research activities in recent times, both theoretically and experimentally, due to their unique physical properties and association with open quantum systems. We show that modular structures, where specific couplings at regular intervals take distinct values, enrich the unique topological attributes of these systems such as the non-Hermitian skin effect and the breakdown of conventional bulk-boundary correspondence. These systems also possess the capability of displaying criticality-enhanced sensitivity for precision metrology. We establish how the modular structure enhances their sensing performance near spectral topological phase transitions and show that the enhancement can be achieved in multi-parameter estimation scenarios as well.
tldr: This paper studies modular non-Hermitian topological systems and their enhanced sensing near spectral topological phase transitions.
motivation: Non-Hermitian topological systems have unique properties like skin effect and breakdown of bulk-boundary correspondence; modular structures may enrich these and improve sensing.
method: The authors theoretically analyze modular non-Hermitian Hamiltonians with periodic distinct couplings, studying topological phases and sensitivity near phase transitions.
result: Modular structures enhance the non-Hermitian skin effect and sensing performance in both single- and multi-parameter estimation scenarios.
conclusion: The work opens avenues for using modular non-Hermitian topology in precision metrology and quantum sensing.

title: A Variational Quantum Algorithm For Nonlinear Finite Element Analysis Of Hyperelastic Materials
authors: Caglar Oskay Uditnarayan Kouskiya
abstract: ArXiv:2605.29181v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This manuscript explores a variational quantum formulation for nonlinear elasticity problems arising from hyperelastic material models, targeting near term noisy intermediate scale quantum (NISQ) devices. The approach leverages the potential energy structure of hyperelasticity and employs a hybrid quantum classical framework in which the energy functional is evaluated using parameterized quantum circuits and optimized through classical routines. To enable implementation on current quantum hardware, polynomial approximations of the nonlinear strain energy density are introduced, yielding a representation compatible with variational quantum algorithms. The methodology is demonstrated on a one dimensional NeoHookean material model using finite element discretizations with first and second order shape functions and nonhomogeneous boundary conditions. Numerical experiments investigate the influence of the polynomial approximation order on the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed approach, illustrating its feasibility for near term quantum devices.
tldr: This paper proposes a variational quantum algorithm for nonlinear finite element analysis of hyperelastic materials, using polynomial approximations to enable NISQ implementation.
motivation: To explore quantum computing for solving nonlinear elasticity problems, which are computationally intensive for classical methods, and to demonstrate feasibility on near-term quantum devices.
method: A hybrid quantum-classical framework where the hyperelastic energy functional is evaluated using parameterized quantum circuits with polynomial approximations of the strain energy density, optimized classically.
result: Numerical experiments on a 1D NeoHookean model show that the polynomial approximation order affects accuracy and efficiency, and the approach is feasible for NISQ devices.
conclusion: The work suggests that variational quantum algorithms can be applied to nonlinear finite element analysis, but further research is needed for higher dimensions and more complex materials.

title: Hybrid Gaussian-exponential Zero-noise Extrapolation For Periodic Circuits
authors: Yun Shang Tao Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.29242v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Zero-noise extrapolation provides a practical means of suppressing gate errors in current noisy intermediate-scale quantum hardware. The accuracy of the zero-noise estimate depends sensitively on the fidelity of the assumed noise model to the actual error scaling. This work introduces a hybrid Gaussian-exponential extrapolation scheme tailored for quantum circuits with periodic structure, which are ubiquitous in quantum algorithms. Under Pauli diagonal errors, by constructing and analyzing an approximate Markov process for the transfer of Pauli operators, we prove a central limit theorem: the noise amplification factor weakly approaches a log-normal distribution, which motivates augmenting the standard exponential model with Gaussian variance corrections. The resulting model requires no prior noise characterization and applies directly to arbitrary periodic circuits. Performance is assessed on Trotterized Ising dynamics, random circuits, and Grover search algorithm using Qiskit noise simulators. For moderate to large circuit depths, the hybrid model yields measurable reductions in bias relative to previous extrapolation variants, indicating its utility for error mitigation on near-term quantum hardware.
tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid Gaussian-exponential zero-noise extrapolation method for error mitigation in periodic quantum circuits, demonstrating reduced bias in simulations.
motivation: Zero-noise extrapolation accuracy depends on noise model fidelity; periodic circuits exhibit noise amplification that deviates from simple exponential scaling, motivating a more accurate model.
method: The authors model Pauli error transfer as an approximate Markov process, prove a central limit theorem for noise amplification factor approaching log-normal distribution, and combine exponential and Gaussian corrections into a hybrid extrapolation scheme.
result: The hybrid model reduces bias compared to standard exponential extrapolation in Trotterized Ising dynamics, random circuits, and Grover search simulations on Qiskit noise simulators.
conclusion: The method improves error mitigation for periodic circuits without prior noise characterization, but its applicability to non-Pauli errors and experimental hardware remains to be tested.

title: Permutation Matrix Representation For Quantum Simulation: Comparative Resource Analysis
authors: Itay Hen Hriday Sabharwal
abstract: ArXiv:2605.29279v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a comparative study of the permutation matrix representation (PMR) method for Hamiltonian simulation alongside other leading quantum algorithms. Our analysis focuses on resource costs for simulating both time-independent and time-dependent Hamiltonians. For the time-independent case, we benchmark PMR against quantum signal processing (QSP) and qubitization, using the Rydberg interaction Hamiltonian as a representative example. For the time-dependent case, we compare the time-dependent extension of PMR with the quantum highly oscillatory protocol (qHOP), applied to a Floquet-driven transverse field Ising model in arbitrary spatial dimensions. In both regimes, we find that PMR offers complementary advantages in resource requirements and exhibits favorable scaling with certain system parameters, suggesting that it may provide practical benefits on resource-constrained quantum hardware.
tldr: This paper compares the permutation matrix representation method for Hamiltonian simulation against QSP and qubitization, showing complementary resource advantages.
motivation: To evaluate the resource efficiency of a new Hamiltonian simulation method (PMR) for both time-independent and time-dependent Hamiltonians, aiming to identify practical benefits for near-term quantum hardware.
method: Benchmarking PMR against quantum signal processing and qubitization for time-independent case (Rydberg Hamiltonian) and against qHOP for time-dependent case (Floquet-driven transverse field Ising model), analyzing gate counts and qubit requirements.
result: PMR offers complementary advantages in resource requirements and favorable scaling with certain system parameters compared to existing methods.
conclusion: PMR may provide practical benefits on resource-constrained quantum hardware, but the paper does not directly address information thermodynamics, quantum foundations, communication, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Scale-free Density Bound For Gaussian Maxima
authors: Suhas Vijaykumar
abstract: ArXiv:2605.29066v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive a scale-free bound on the density of the maximum of a centered Gaussian vector. The basic bound is non-uniform, depends logarithmically on the dimension, and allows any covariance matrix. When the largest marginal variance is separated from zero, it implies that the density of the maximum is uniformly controlled at all quantiles above 2/3, which is sufficient for many hypothesis testing applications; it yields validity of Gaussian and bootstrap approximations for maxima of high-dimensional sums at test levels [MATH] without further restricting the covariance. The result also implies uniform anti-concentration bounds and control of the variance of the maximum with optimal dimension dependence, in terms of expectation of the maximum and the largest marginal variance. We discuss implications for high-dimensional correlation testing, time-uniform sequential testing, and non-parametric inference under latent, low-dimensional structure.
tldr: The paper derives a scale-free bound on the density of the maximum of a centered Gaussian vector, with applications in high-dimensional statistics and hypothesis testing.
motivation: To obtain non-asymptotic bounds on the density of Gaussian maxima that are uniform over covariance structures, enabling valid Gaussian and bootstrap approximations for high-dimensional inference.
method: Analytical derivation using properties of Gaussian processes and extreme value theory, yielding a non-uniform bound that depends logarithmically on dimension.
result: A scale-free density bound that controls the density of the maximum at quantiles above 2/3, with optimal dimension dependence in terms of expectation and largest marginal variance.
conclusion: The results have implications for high-dimensional correlation testing, time-uniform sequential testing, and non-parametric inference under latent low-dimensional structure.

title: Dead Zones Enable Flexible Phase Organization In Coupled Oscillators
authors: Ruby Kim Naghmeh Akhavan
abstract: ArXiv:2605.29167v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coupled oscillator networks underlie many biological systems, from cardiac cycles to circadian rhythms. Phase-reduced models such as the Kuramoto model have been widely used to study synchronization, but they typically assume that oscillators remain continuously responsive to inputs and often produce tightly clustered phase distributions. Biological oscillators, however, commonly exhibit phase intervals during which inputs have little or no effect, called ``dead zones." Here, we extend the Kuramoto model by introducing receiver-gated dead zones, in which oscillators transiently ignore incoming signals. Using analytical and numerical approaches, we show that dead zones can reduce synchronization rates, modulate the distribution of phase-locked solutions, and modify the stability of phase-locked states. For identical oscillators, full synchrony remains locally exponentially stable and numerically dominant, although convergence times depend sensitively on the dead-zone width. For heterogeneous oscillators that admit phase-locked solutions when the coupling strength satisfies [MATH], dead zones broaden the long-term phase distributions. Numerical exploration across dead zone widths reveals a transition in which steady phase gaps lose stability, resulting in dead zone-induced phase drifting. Overall, these results identify phase-response dead zones as a biologically plausible mechanism for flexible phase organization beyond classical Kuramoto dynamics.
tldr: This paper extends the Kuramoto model by introducing receiver-gated dead zones to study flexible phase organization in coupled oscillators.
motivation: Biological oscillators often exhibit phase intervals where inputs have little effect, but standard phase-reduced models assume continuous responsiveness and produce tightly clustered phase distributions.
method: The authors extend the Kuramoto model with receiver-gated dead zones and use analytical and numerical approaches to study synchronization, phase-locked solutions, and stability.
result: Dead zones reduce synchronization rates, broaden phase distributions in heterogeneous oscillators, and can induce phase drifting; full synchrony remains stable for identical oscillators but convergence times depend on dead-zone width.
conclusion: Phase-response dead zones provide a biologically plausible mechanism for flexible phase organization, with implications for biological systems like circadian rhythms and cardiac cycles.

title: Quantum Implicit-Explicit Schemes For Multiscale Ordinary And Partial Differential Equations Via Schr\"odingerization
authors: Qitong Hu, Xiaoyang He, Shi Jin, Xiao-Dong Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.29423v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we present a quantum implicit-explicit (IMEX) scheme for multiscale ordinary and partial differential equations whose discretization parameters are independent of the scaling parameter [MATH]. A key ingredient of our approach is a continuous-time formulation of classical IMEX schemes, which decouples the evolution time of the quantum algorithm from the physical time of the differential equation and is therefore particularly useful in multiscale settings. Building on this idea, we employ the Schr\"odingerization framework [Phys. Rev. Lett. 133 (2024), 230602] to implement IMEX schemes on quantum computers. Compared to previous HHL type quantum AP scheme [J. Comput. Phys. 471 (2022), 111641], this new method requires narrower -- an extra logarithmic factor -- auxiliary register numerical examples on linear heat and multiscale telegraph equations demonstrate the independence in [MATH] of the method.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum IMEX scheme for multiscale ODEs/PDEs using Schrödingerization, but it is not directly related to the user's research interests in quantum information thermodynamics, foundations, communication, or hybrid systems.
motivation: To develop quantum algorithms for multiscale differential equations that avoid dependence on the scaling parameter, improving efficiency over classical methods.
method: A continuous-time formulation of classical IMEX schemes is combined with the Schrödingerization framework to map the problem to a Schrödinger equation, enabling implementation on quantum computers.
result: The method requires only an extra logarithmic factor in auxiliary register size compared to previous HHL-type schemes, and numerical examples on linear heat and multiscale telegraph equations show independence of the scaling parameter.
conclusion: The approach offers a promising quantum algorithm for multiscale problems, but its relevance to the user's specific interests is limited.

title: User-Centric Clustering For uRLLC In Cell-Free Ran Via Extreme Value Theory
authors: Yu Zhang, Xinyue Yang, Dongming Wang, Boyou Yi, Yaqin Xie, Hua Zhou, Zhizhong Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.29441v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ultra-reliable low-latency communication (uRLLC) is a pivotal enabler for B5G/6G networks, yet it faces severe challenges from rare but critical extreme events, which are characterized by heavy tails in the delay distribution. While the cell-free radio access network (CF-RAN) architecture offers essential spatial diversity to combat these uncertainties, conventional user-centric clustering designs typically focus on average metrics, thereby inadequately addressing such tail behaviors. We propose a novel, tail-risk-aware, user-centric clustering framework operating within the finite blocklength (FBL) regime. Our approach employs extreme value theory (EVT), specifically the peaks-over-threshold (POT) model, to accurately quantify the probability of queue latency violations. This framework is applied to formulate an energy efficiency (EE) maximization problem under strict tail latency constraints. The problem is solved via an efficient online algorithm that integrates Lyapunov optimization with successive convex approximation (SCA). Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme, through its dynamic adaptation of cluster formation to mitigate tail risks, achieves a superior reliability-efficiency trade-off and leads to a significant suppression of extreme latency events.
tldr: This paper proposes a user-centric clustering framework for ultra-reliable low-latency communication in cell-free RAN using extreme value theory to manage tail latency risks.
motivation: Conventional clustering designs focus on average metrics and fail to address rare extreme events that cause heavy tails in delay distribution, which is critical for uRLLC in B5G/6G.
method: The framework uses peaks-over-threshold (POT) model from extreme value theory to quantify queue latency violation probabilities, and solves an energy efficiency maximization problem under tail latency constraints via Lyapunov optimization and successive convex approximation.
result: The proposed scheme dynamically adapts cluster formation to mitigate tail risks, achieving a superior reliability-efficiency trade-off and significant suppression of extreme latency events.
conclusion: The work demonstrates the effectiveness of EVT for tail-aware resource allocation in CF-RAN, with potential extensions to other network optimization problems.

title: Secure Distributed Hypothesis Testing
authors: Gowtham R. Kurri, Varun Narayanan, Vinod M. Prabhakaran, K. R. Sahasranand
abstract: ArXiv:2605.29760v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In distributed hypothesis testing, a central server performs hypothesis testing based on information received from distributed sensors/clients. We study a secure variant of this problem in which the central server determines the hypothesis class of an underlying distribution without learning any additional information about the distribution itself. We prove that, in its standard form, this is impossible to achieve, even for simple and highly restricted cases. To bypass this impossibility, we augment the model with a shared secret key available to clients but hidden from the server. We show that a single-bit secret key enables perfectly secure testing for simple classes by reducing the test distributions to a symmetric, canonical instance. Finally, for arbitrary hypothesis classes over finite domains, we establish a reduction to standard hypothesis testing using Private Simultaneous Messages (PSM) protocols, achieving polynomial communication and key lengths.
